topic_tag: an island port held by an empire
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.

worlds.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait on the main sea route to its eastern provinces. The empire's fleets on that route could carry only a few weeks of water and grain, and for four months of storms each year no merchant ship would sail it. All summer, merchant ships unloaded grain, salted meat, and spare timber on the island's quays and sailed home empty. Each winter the fleets put in at the island and left it fully loaded. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
worlds.explanation: Goods arrive on the island in summer, when merchants can sail, and the fleets load them in winter, when merchants cannot; combining the two shows the goods were kept there between seasons, so the empire valued the island as its "storehouse." "Tollgate" fails because ships were supplied at the island, not charged for passing it. "Watchtower" fails because nothing in this account depends on seeing from the island. "Trophy" fails because the fleets could not have made the crossing without what the island held.

tollgate.why: the fleets took goods from the island; nothing was collected from ships for passage

watchtower.quote: unloaded grain, salted meat, and spare timber
watchtower.why: the island's role in this mechanism is receiving and giving out supplies, not observation

trophy.quote: could carry only a few weeks of water
trophy.why: the fleets depended on the island in practice, so it was not kept for show

worlds.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait on the main sea route to its eastern provinces. At the island the strait narrows to a channel one ship wide, close beneath the harbor. Every merchant ship's master went ashore at the island's harbor office and returned with a stamped paper before sailing on, and the empire's patrol at the strait's far end turned back any ship without one. The treasury's ledgers show that the office's receipts paid for the empire's whole navy in those waters. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
worlds.explanation: Ships could only use the strait with a paper bought at the island's harbor office, and those receipts funded a navy, so the empire valued the island as its "tollgate." "Storehouse" fails because ships sailed on with their cargo after getting the paper. "Watchtower" fails because the island's role was charging ships for passage, not watching for enemies. "Trophy" fails because the island produced large revenues.

storehouse.quote: returned with a stamped paper before sailing on
storehouse.why: ships left with their cargo; nothing was kept on the island

watchtower.quote: the office's receipts paid for the empire's whole navy
watchtower.why: the island's value was money taken from passing trade, not warning of attack

trophy.why: an island earning a navy's cost is valued for income, not as a symbol

worlds.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait on the main sea route to its eastern provinces. The island's single hill rises higher than any point on the mainland coast for a hundred miles. The garrison kept a beacon laid ready on its summit, matched by beacons on headlands along the coast as far as the capital. Twice in the century an enemy fleet sailing for the capital found the empire's ships already gathered and waiting for it. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
worlds.explanation: The high hill, the chain of beacons to the capital, and the enemy fleets that found the empire's ships ready combine to show the island gave early warning of attack, so the empire valued it as its "watchtower." "Storehouse" fails because no goods move through the island in this account. "Tollgate" fails because no ship is stopped or charged. "Trophy" fails because the island's warning did real military work.

storehouse.why: the island's value lies in its height for seeing and signaling, not in anything kept there

tollgate.why: the island's link to the mainland is a signal chain, not a charge on shipping

trophy.quote: found the empire's ships already gathered
trophy.why: the warning had practical effect, so the island was not merely a prize

worlds.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait on the main sea route to its eastern provinces. Within twenty years the strait silted up so that no ship larger than a fishing boat could pass, and the sea route moved to a deeper channel. Afterward only the garrison's supply boat called. The empire still spent more on the island's garrison than on any province, carried its keys in procession each anniversary of its capture, and hung a painting of its harbor behind the throne. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
worlds.explanation: Once the strait silted up, the island lay on no route and served no practical purpose, while the empire paid heavily to hold it and celebrated its capture, so the empire valued it as its "trophy." "Storehouse" fails because only the garrison's own boat called. "Tollgate" fails because ships no longer passed the island. "Watchtower" fails because no fleet could use the silted strait, so there was nothing there to watch for.

storehouse.quote: only the garrison's supply boat called
storehouse.why: no fleet called to be supplied, so the island held nothing for anyone

tollgate.quote: the sea route moved to a deeper channel
tollgate.why: with the route gone, there was no passing trade to charge

watchtower.quote: no ship larger than a fishing boat could pass
watchtower.why: an enemy fleet could not come through the strait, so a lookout there guarded nothing
